title: The colour of a roof
bodyMd:
On a still summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the farmland around it. Asphalt and dark roofing absorb most of the sunlight that falls on them, store it, and give it back slowly through the evening, so streets that bake by day keep the city warm long after sunset. A shortage of trees makes matters worse: fewer trees mean less shade and less of the cooling that comes from water evaporating from leaves.

The cheapest remedy appears to be a coat of paint. A roof finished in a pale, reflective coating sends back much of the sunlight that a black roof would absorb, and on a hot day its surface can be twenty or more degrees cooler. When one southern town repainted the roofs of forty of its own buildings, staff on the top floors reported cooler rooms, and the electricity used for air conditioning in those buildings fell the following summer.

The results, however, are less tidy than the slogan "paint it white" suggests. A reflective roof also turns away the winter sun, whose warmth would have been welcome, so in colder climates part of the summer saving is cancelled by extra heating. The coating loses much of its effect as dust and soot settle on it, unless someone cleans it. And pale pavements, tried on a few streets, created a difficulty of their own: the sunlight they reflect does not disappear but strikes passers-by and the walls of nearby buildings, so a pedestrian can feel hotter on a pale street than on a dark one even though the ground beneath is cooler.

None of this makes reflective surfaces a bad idea; it makes them a local one. Whether they help depends on the climate, on whether anyone will maintain them, and on how high the surface sits above the people it is meant to protect. A roof ten storeys up can return sunlight to the sky without harming anyone; a pavement at street level cannot. The question a city should ask is not which colour is coolest but where the reflected heat will go.
